name: Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946)
info: The kingdom without a king that the Regent Miklós Horthy ruled from 1920 to 1946, shaped by the losses of the Treaty of Trianon, which joined the Axis and took part in the Holocaust.

facts.founder: A coalition of right-wing political forces, with Miklós Horthy chosen as regent on 1 March 1920
facts.predecessor: The Hungarian Democratic Republic and the Hungarian Soviet Republic, after the dissolution of Austria-Hungary
facts.successor: The Second Hungarian Republic (1946), followed by the Hungarian People's Republic (1949)

t: The Treaty of Trianon of 1920 cost Hungary 72% of its historical territory and 58% of its population, and left more than three million ethnic Hungarians outside its borders.
Hungary was a kingdom without royalty: after the Diet dethroned Charles IV in 1921, Miklós Horthy ruled as regent until the Germans overthrew him in 1944.
As an Axis power Hungary regained Hungarian-majority lands, and in 1944 Hungarian authorities deported hundreds of thousands of Jews to Nazi concentration camps, where most of them died.
dyk: The prime minister Gyula Gömbös is said to have coined the word "axis" for the alliance he wanted with Germany and Italy, and the two countries used it for their Rome–Berlin axis.
ev: A coalition of right-wing forces restores the monarchy, and Miklós Horthy is chosen regent on 1 March
Hungary signs the Treaty of Trianon on 4 June, losing Transylvania, much of Upper Hungary and Vojvodina
Charles IV fails to retake the throne, and the Diet abolishes the House of Habsburg's rights to it
The First Vienna Award returns the southern parts of Czechoslovakia to Hungary
The Second Vienna Award assigns Northern Transylvania to Hungary
Hungary joins the invasion of Yugoslavia and, on 27 June, declares war on the Soviet Union
Germany occupies Hungary in March, and in October overthrows Horthy and installs Ferenc Szálasi of the Arrow Cross Party
The monarchy is formally abolished on 1 February and replaced by the Second Hungarian Republic

sections.foundation:
After Austria-Hungary dissolved at the end of the First World War, the Hungarian Democratic Republic and then the Hungarian Soviet Republic were proclaimed in 1918 and 1919. Béla Kun's communist government launched the "Red Terror" and drew Hungary into a war with Romania. In 1920 anti-communists and monarchists purged communists, leftist intellectuals and others they saw as threats, above all Jews, in the "White Terror". After the last Romanian occupation forces left, a coalition of right-wing forces restored Hungary as a constitutional monarchy on 29 February 1920.

The Allies would not accept a return of the Habsburgs, and Archduke Joseph August, who had declared himself regent, stood down after two weeks. On 1 March 1920 Miklós Horthy, the last commanding admiral of the Austro-Hungarian Navy, was chosen regent, with Sándor Simonyi-Semadam as his first prime minister. In 1921 King Charles IV tried to retake the throne, even marching on Budapest with rebel troops in October, but the army stayed loyal to Horthy and Charles was exiled to Madeira. On 6 November 1921 the Diet nullified the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 and abolished the Habsburgs' rights to the throne.
sections.socioeconomy:
The loss of agricultural and industrial lands at Trianon brought economic decline, budget deficits and high inflation and left Hungary dependent on farm exports. Prime Minister István Bethlen's government stabilised the currency with large foreign loans and introduced the pengő in 1927, and industry, farming and trade grew for most of the 1920s. The Great Depression and the failure of the Creditanstalt bank in Vienna ended the boom, and from the mid-1930s Hungary's economy came to depend on Germany's.

Society was split into two worlds. Budapest had a standard of living roughly equal to Western Europe's, while most of the countryside was very poor and many peasants could not read; on the Great Hungarian Plain half a million people lived on isolated farms, the tanya, without roads or schools. A small nobility owned most of the land. The census of 1920 found that Jews made up 6% of the population; never regarded as "gentlemen" in a society obsessed with status, they were strongly represented in business and the professions. The education minister Kuno von Klebelsberg built 3,500 rural elementary schools, but admitted that the state could not afford enough schools to end rural illiteracy.
sections.military:
Hungary's army served its policy of revision. In April 1941 Hungary let the Wehrmacht cross its territory for the invasion of Yugoslavia, joined the operations and annexed the Bačka region of Vojvodina and Muraköz. On 27 June 1941 László Bárdossy declared war on the Soviet Union, and, fearing that German support might turn to the Romanians, the government sent forces to Operation Barbarossa. The support cost the Hungarians dearly: almost the entire Second Army of the Royal Hungarian Army was lost at the Battle of Stalingrad.

From 1941 Romani men were forced into the Labour Service battalions of the Honvéd, where, the historian Katalin Katz noted, they were at the mercy of merciless and often sadistic officers and many died. When Hungary tried to leave the war in 1944, Germany invaded in Operation Margarethe on 19 March, meeting little resistance, and in October Operation Panzerfaust removed Horthy. The Red Army reached Budapest in November 1944 and laid siege to it; the city capitulated in February 1945. The Debrecen government began forming a new army to fight on the Soviet side, but the volunteers made up only small units, the largest being the Volunteer Regiment of Buda.
sections.governance:
Horthy's rule could be construed as a dictatorship, though his powers continued those of the King of Hungary: he could adjourn or dissolve the Diet at his discretion and appointed the prime minister. The succession was never settled; in January 1942 Parliament made his eldest son István deputy regent, but István was killed in a plane crash that August. István Deák described a rightist country ruled by a small clique of aristocrats, civil servants and army officers, which saw itself as a bulwark against Bolshevism.

Under Bethlen open voting was brought back outside Budapest and the larger cities, and his Party of Unity won repeated elections. The numerus clausus law of 1920, passed under Pál Teleki, limited Jewish university students to 5%; Bethlen relaxed it in 1928, but Gyula Gömbös and Bálint Hóman restored it after antisemitic student demonstrations from 1932. Gömbös moved Hungary towards one-party rule on the Italian and German model, and the "Jewish Laws" first limited Jews to 20 percent in a number of professions. In 1944 the pro-Nazi Döme Sztójay legalised the Arrow Cross Party, and Ferenc Szálasi, installed in October, ruled as "Leader of the Nation".
sections.impact:
Revision of the Treaty of Trianon dominated Hungary's politics and foreign policy, and the resentment it caused has lasted to the present. Hungary signed a treaty of friendship with Mussolini's Italy on 5 April 1927, and Gömbös acted as intermediary between Germany and Italy. Through the First Vienna Award it regained southern Czechoslovakia, then occupied the Carpatho-Ukraine, and through the Second Vienna Award it gained Northern Transylvania, before joining the Axis powers. Richard Griffiths argues that its economic dependence on Germany, its antisemitic laws and its part in the killing of its Jews place it within international fascism.

From May to June 1944 Hungarian authorities rounded up hundreds of thousands of Jews and sent them to Nazi concentration camps, where most died; in northern Transylvania many Jews who had welcomed Hungarian rule in 1940 were deported by Hungarian gendarmes to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Arrow Cross militias murdered 10,000–15,000 Jews. Romani people were massacred by the Arrow Cross, forced into over 30 work camps and deported to Dachau, Bergen-Belsen and Ravensbrück. Despite strict censorship, Deák called the era "a golden age of literature and art" in Budapest.
sections.decline:
By early 1944 Hungary was secretly seeking an armistice with the Allies. When Germany learned of it, it occupied the country on 19 March, put Horthy under house arrest and replaced Prime Minister Miklós Kállay with Döme Sztójay, who governed with the aid of a Nazi military governor, Edmund Veesenmayer. In August Horthy removed Sztójay and appointed Géza Lakatos, but when Hungary again tried to leave the war in October the Germans kidnapped Horthy's son, forced Horthy to resign and installed Ferenc Szálasi's Government of National Unity, which fought on beside the Axis.

On 21 December 1944 an Interim Assembly met in Debrecen with Soviet approval and elected a counter-government under Béla Miklós, former commander of the Hungarian First Army. It declared war on Germany, concluded an armistice with the Allies, set up People's Tribunals and carried out a land reform in March 1945, under the Allied Control Commission led by Marshal Kliment Voroshilov. Szálasi's government, in exile in Munich, was disbanded in May 1945. A High National Council served as head of state until the monarchy was formally abolished on 1 February 1946, and the Second Hungarian Republic was soon followed by the communist Hungarian People's Republic.

summary: The Kingdom of Hungary of 1920 to 1946 was a monarchy without a king, ruled by the Regent Miklós Horthy and a conservative, nationalist and fiercely anti-communist elite. Driven to revise the Treaty of Trianon, it joined the Axis, regained lost lands, persecuted its Jews and Romani and took part in the Holocaust, before German and then Soviet occupation ended it.
references: Deborah S. Cornelius, Hungary in World War II: Caught in the Cauldron (Fordham University Press, 2011)
Andrew Janos, The Politics of Backwardness in Hungary, 1825–1945 (Princeton University Press, 2012)
Ferenc Laczó, Hungarian Jews in the Age of Genocide: An Intellectual History, 1929–1948 (Brill, 2016)
Jekatyerina Dunajeva, Constructing Identities over Time: "Bad Gypsies" and "Good Roma" in Russia and Hungary (Central European University Press, 2021)

pointDescs.1920: Horthy is chosen regent on 1 March, and the Treaty of Trianon of 4 June strips Hungary of 72% of its historical territory.
pointDescs.1921: Charles IV's attempts to retake the throne fail, and on 6 November the Diet abolishes the Habsburgs' rights, confirming Horthy as regent.
pointDescs.1927: After Bethlen's stabilisation, the pengő is introduced and Hungary signs a treaty of friendship with Italy, while industry and trade flourish.
pointDescs.1931: The economic collapse of 1929–1931 forces Bethlen to resign as prime minister.
pointDescs.1938: The First Vienna Award returns the southern parts of Czechoslovakia to Hungary.
pointDescs.1940: The Second Vienna Award assigns Northern Transylvania to Hungary, which then joins the Axis powers.
pointDescs.1941: Hungary joins the invasion of Yugoslavia, annexes the Bačka and Muraköz, and declares war on the Soviet Union on 27 June.
pointDescs.1944: Germany occupies Hungary in March; hundreds of thousands of Jews are deported, and in October the Germans replace Horthy with Szálasi.
pointDescs.1945: Budapest capitulates in February, and Szálasi's government in exile is disbanded at the end of May.
pointDescs.1946: The monarchy is formally abolished on 1 February and replaced by the Second Hungarian Republic.
